# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming*, second edition [@Dijkstra1970Notes, p. 7]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *How do returned signals become trustworthy, what do they mean for the architecture work, and what should improve or be retained as a result?*

**Core thesis:** *Raw tool returns must be qualified through verification before feedback can guide the next design action and accumulate into durable learning across runs.*
:::

A clean simulator exit or a zero-violation timing report is not proof of a working chip; raw tool returns become architectural evidence only when qualified against physical constraints, operating corners, and formal invariants. An optimizer that reads tool logs at face value will exploit whatever the check omits: an unjustified `set_false_path` exception removes a real setup violation from the timing report, an unconstrained multicycle path hides a slow divider, and an idealized zero-delay memory model credits a candidate with bandwidth it does not have. Each omission produces a reported gain that the hardware cannot deliver.

To keep an optimization loop from chasing false gains, this chapter first separates infrastructure failures, such as a license timeout or memory exhaustion, from design failures, such as a protocol deadlock or a setup violation. It then follows a qualified tool return into the next design action and into the records that later runs should retain (@fig-ch07-cover-map).

This qualification step builds directly on machine-usable representations (@sec-data-representations-world-models), method choice (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), and isolated execution environments (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). Whereas the execution environment establishes that a run executed as recorded, verification establishes what that run actually proves before its evidence guides redesign or retirement, and @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect evaluates the resulting workflow against human baselines.

![**Qualifying returned signals into actionable feedback and retained learning.** Raw tool outputs pass through verification qualification to establish their validity envelope and bounded claims. Feedback routes the qualified evidence to guide revisions, further checks, or stopping decisions, while durable observations are retained for cross-run learning.](images/ch07-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch07-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a returned signal passes through verification qualification and a bounded claim before feedback routes the next action and learning is retained."}

## Turning Tool Feedback into Qualified Design Actions {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

Generating register-transfer level (RTL) candidates and establishing that they meet their requirements are different jobs. Even when a tool run finishes cleanly, it can leave an unhandled multicycle path,[^fn-mcp-c07] an unconstrained power domain, or a floating CMOS node[^fn-floating-cmos-c07] unexamined. An AI-native design system must therefore determine what its tool returns actually reveal about a candidate and how those findings should guide redesign.

[^fn-mcp-c07]: **Multicycle paths**: A sequential path designed to require more than one clock cycle between launch and capture registers (such as complex floating-point or multi-cycle divider units). Static timing analysis tools default to enforcing single-cycle timing; an unhandled multicycle path triggers false timing violations, while an erroneous `set_multicycle_path` constraint hides true setup failures by permitting unvalidated extra clock cycles.

[^fn-floating-cmos-c07]: **Floating CMOS Node**: A condition where a CMOS gate input is not driven by any defined logic level (0 or 1), leaving its voltage uncontrolled. An intermediate input voltage can turn on both input transistors, increasing static current; noise can also produce unpredictable logic transitions.

Whereas the execution environment in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces supplies immutable records with pinned dependencies and raw transcripts, qualification determines which architectural claims those returns can support, and the target claim decides which check is required. Empirical checks qualify observed performance and physical quantities from cycle-accurate simulations, hardware emulators, or post-silicon telemetry. Formal methods, by contrast, prove that a mathematical model satisfies its invariants under declared assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking], though even a completed formal run must be checked to confirm that the solver proved the intended obligation.

Before raw execution logs can guide an architectural choice, each return must pass through a sequence of qualification steps, any of which can send the work back rather than forward (@fig-evidence-flow).

![**Tool returns gain architectural meaning through claim-specific result qualification.** Execution records supply returns with status and lineage; result qualification binds types, targets, and conditions; property checks test formal or physical validity; and feedback scoping defines supported claims before learning records what to revise or retain.](images/fig-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow width="80%" fig-alt="Five-step flow diagram from tool return through verification and a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

A return reaches the design state only after it answers five separate questions:

1. Did the requested tool run execute to completion without infrastructure faults or license drops?
2. Is the returned artifact structurally and syntactically valid for downstream toolchains?
3. Is the measurement or proof valid under its declared model and assumptions, including relevant process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions?
4. Which specific architectural requirement or physical constraint does the result satisfy or contradict, and which requirements remain unexamined?
5. What concrete design revision, parameter update, further check, or bounded claim does the qualified evidence support? Does it instead justify retaining the candidate or stopping work on it?

Answering these questions in order determines what should change next. While the execution harness in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces confirms that the tool ran cleanly (isolating process exits, license drops, and memory exhaustion), verification in this chapter checks what the hardware result means (exposing false slack paths, unconstrained clocks, and vacuous formal assertions). A license timeout calls for infrastructure recovery; it says nothing about whether the candidate design is flawed.

When a candidate instead encounters a genuine, qualified physical or timing violation, an autonomous loop should not discard the design and restart generative exploration blindly. A useful starting point is a *causal repair hierarchy*, ordered by how much of the architecture each fix disturbs, though the cost and suitability of any repair still depend on the specific violation:

1. *Localized physical ECO (lowest disruption).* Gate sizing, threshold-voltage ($V_t$) swapping, buffer insertion, and pin swapping. These physical engineering change orders close near-miss negative slack paths without altering the RTL or sequential behavior, and a parameter optimizer can automate them within a fixed netlist.
2. *Sequential retiming and pipelining (moderate disruption).* Moving flip-flops across combinational boundaries or inserting pipeline registers on latency-insensitive paths. These transformations require sequential equivalence checking (SEC) under the intended cycle correspondence. Added latency is permissible only where the interface contract allows it; otherwise the contract and its dependent checks also need revision.
3. *Structural and algorithmic redesign (highest disruption).* Decomposing wide arbiters, splitting monolithic crossbars into distributed networks-on-chip, replacing cache tag arrays with software-managed scratchpads, or synthesizing redundant carry-save arithmetic. This tier can invalidate existing floorplans and require changes across architectural and physical representations.

Lower-disruption repairs deserve consideration whenever they can satisfy the relevant constraints at acceptable cost, whereas other diagnoses justify immediate structural redesign or stopping altogether, for example when an interface bandwidth limit rules out local timing repair or an ECO would exceed the power budget. What a repair loop can attempt also depends on the scope of its search: a search confined to a fixed parameter template can apply only the fixes its action space represents, because an optimizer facing saturated pin bandwidth or unclosable timing cannot redesign a microarchitecture outside that template (@sec-routing-evidence-layers returns to what each class of workflow can do with returned evidence). Whenever a repair does alter the structure, it must requalify every check that the change invalidates, and an automated repair loop must still beat conventional human-led repair at comparable total cost, because that is the engineering work it would replace.

How a run fails or what it omits also shapes qualification before any repair begins. An interrupted run may still supply completed measurements or proofs whose lineage, completion status, and scope can be established independently of the interrupted step, whereas outputs whose status remains uncertain are retained only as partial records because no incomplete return can discharge a verification obligation. Missing checks and demonstrated violations require similarly distinct responses even though both block a full feasibility claim: omitting a required PVT corner or a Unified Power Format (UPF)[^fn-upf-c07] isolation check leaves that timing or power-state behavior unqualified until the check runs, whereas a completed check that catches an isolation failure provides direct evidence of a design or power-intent defect.

[^fn-upf-c07]: **Unified Power Format (UPF)**: The standard declarative specification language for low-power design intent, defining power domains, supply nets, power-switch networks, isolation cells, and level shifters. Modern toolchains decouple logical RTL from physical power intent; RTL simulation cannot verify power-gating sequences or domain transitions without companion UPF constraints and power-state tables.

## Why Candidates That Pass Early Simulators Fail at Signoff {#sec-signal-sources-attrition}

The checks that produce these returns span a wide range of latency, spatial granularity, and physical fidelity. Analytical roofline estimators can evaluate simple kernels in milliseconds, whereas cycle-accurate simulation and full-chip physical signoff may take hours, and hardware emulation trades compilation time for execution speed by running long instruction traces far faster than software simulation. Across electronic design automation (EDA) engines, static timing, dynamic IR-drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c07] and design rule checking likewise diagnose different physical failure modes: an IR-drop report from RedHawk-SC locates a voltage droop on the die, while Cadence Tempus isolates a failing timing path. Neither report by itself names which upstream architectural choice should change, but lineage that binds each metric to candidate parameters, RTL revisions, tool flags, and constraints makes it possible to trace the physical symptom back to its architectural cause.

[^fn-ir-drop-c07]: **Dynamic IR-Drop**: Time-varying switching activity changes current demand on the power-delivery network. The resulting supply-voltage variation can reduce timing margin or threaten stored state. Analysis needs the network and activity models; an ordinary logic simulation does not measure those voltage effects.

Because those high-fidelity signoff checks take hours to return, the latency gap between fast estimates and physical signoff creates a scheduling problem for iterative search. Control theory warns that feedback delay and noise limit how aggressively a controller can respond [@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. Although architectural search is not necessarily a continuous controller and that warning alone does not set a formal stability or latency bound, it highlights the danger of proposing many design changes before their physical consequences return. One practical response is to steer exploration with fast, qualified proxies while slower signoff runs recalibrate those proxies and reopen affected candidates, recording which design revision each delayed result actually checked.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Inline values for the Wilson Research Group sentence below, read from the
# dataset chapter 2 plots in @fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors:
#   data/datasets/chapter7-wilson-verification-scissors-gap.csv
import csv as _csvw7
from pathlib import Path as _Pathw7
import _python.plots as _apw7

_wpath7 = _Pathw7(_apw7.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter7-wilson-verification-scissors-gap.csv"
with open(_wpath7, encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _wrows7 = list(_csvw7.DictReader(l for l in _fh if not l.startswith("#")))
_wv7 = {int(r["study_year"]): int(r["avg_pct_project_time_in_verification"]) for r in _wrows7 if r["avg_pct_project_time_in_verification"]}
_fs7 = {int(r["study_year"]): int(r["first_silicon_success_pct"]) for r in _wrows7 if r["first_silicon_success_pct"]}
wv_min, wv_max = min(_wv7.values()), max(_wv7.values())
```

Managing verification cost and latency is a structural requirement of hardware design rather than a workflow convenience. A sequential circuit with $|S|$ Boolean state bits has at most $2^{|S|}$ possible states, and even when reset and input assumptions restrict the reachable subset, random stimulus can still leave corner-case deadlocks and races unexercised, so adding test vectors alone cannot prove their absence. In the longitudinal Wilson Research Group surveys discussed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, verification consumed an average of `{python} wv_min`% to `{python} wv_max`% of project time from `{python} wv_first` to `{python} wv_last`, while first-silicon success fell to `{python} wv_fs_last`% of projects in `{python} wv_fs_year` [@Foster2013WilsonPart5; @Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Faster candidate generation only widens this gap unless checks matched to each stage filter the candidate pool: evaluation budgets are bounded by available compute and, in commercial flows, by tool license seats, so a generator that sends every raw proposal straight into synthesis and signoff timing wastes scarce licenses on candidates that a parser or linter could have rejected in seconds.

Multi-fidelity screening prevents that waste by organizing verification across progressive tiers of physical fidelity, execution latency, and license expenditure (@fig-synthesis-verification-funnel). Fast parsing, linting, interface compliance, and assertion checks eliminate broken candidates before invoking expensive static timing analysis and physical verification, which in commercial flows also tie up license seats. As the schematic shows, where a failure occurs also determines how the loop recovers. Early syntactic, protocol, and functional rejections route directly back to the generator for prompt revision or abstract syntax tree (AST) repair, whereas late physical timing near-misses can route to localized engineering change order (ECO) iterations (such as buffer insertion, gate sizing, and pin swapping) that close small slack violations without discarding the candidate and restarting the generative loop.

Each tier in this funnel also retains a different amount of diagnostic detail. Early stages often compress surrogate predictions or cycle-simulator outputs into scalar power, performance, and area (PPA) proxies that rank candidates quickly but omit the internal details needed for root-cause diagnosis, even when the underlying simulator can record fuller performance counters and traces on demand. At the narrow bottom of the funnel, static timing analyzers, power-integrity solvers, and design rule checkers instead return specific failing timing paths, spatial current crowding maps, and layout design rule check (DRC) coordinates. @sec-routing-evidence-layers follows each class of signal to the part of the design process that can act on it.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override Top-only placement deferred this tall figure twenty-eight pages past its discussion and blocked later figures. -->
![**Multi-fidelity verification filters generative proposals across progressive fidelity tiers.** Schematic workflow ordering selected checks from fast parsers and linters through static timing and physical verification; the named engines are examples, and their ordering does not specify measured costs or attrition. Its endpoint means that the listed checks passed; additional obligations, including power and thermal checks where required, remain part of the complete verification plan. Closed-loop recovery decouples early structural and functional repairs (routed back to generative prompt revision) from late physical timing near-misses (routed to localized engineering change orders).](images/fig-synthesis-verification-funnel){#fig-synthesis-verification-funnel width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Flowchart of a five-tier multi-fidelity verification signoff funnel from generative candidate proposals down to an implementation passing the listed checks, listing recovery routes for generative repair and localized ECO optimization."}

Because a cheap parser or linter can reject a malformed proposal in seconds, early filtering makes a larger proposal stream affordable, provided each filter is suited to the candidates it screens. Ordering those checks requires weighing what each check can reject, how long it takes, which input artifacts it needs, and how much downstream work a justified rejection saves. A fast check belongs early when its output is strong enough to rule a candidate out, though passing an early check leaves every downstream physical and functional obligation open. Before any empirical measurement from these stages can be compared across candidates, it must also satisfy basic admission criteria.

## Deciding When a Candidate Earns the Next Tool Run {#sec-empirical-admission-criteria}

An empirical measurement cannot enter an architectural comparison until its record establishes exactly what was measured and under what conditions. A clean exit code from a simulator or synthesis run can still hide uninitialized cache warmup states (where cold-start misses distort instructions per cycle), uncalibrated process corners, or truncated trace intervals. The seven record elements in @tbl-measurement-record make these conditions inspectable by identifying the value, recording how it was extracted, and stating the variation and error bounds that limit its use.

| **Record Element** | **Question the record must answer** |
| - | - |
| Candidate identity | Which design revision, hardware configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| Quantity and unit | What architectural metric was computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| Conditions | Which tool and model versions, random-number generator seeds, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions are relevant to this quantity? |
| Extraction status | Did the expected output artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain raw logs? |
| Variation and error | What repetitions, sampling methods, numerical tolerances, or error bounds restrict the value? |
| Constraint integrity | Which versions of applicable timing constraints in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) form, power intent (UPF), and waiver manifests were used, and how are they identified, for example by recorded SHA-256 hashes? |
| Source record | Which returned artifact, extraction procedure, and execution record support this metric, and what dependencies would be needed to reproduce it? |
: **A measurement requires identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These record elements establish whether a measurement is eligible for a scoped comparison; the comparison itself needs additional qualification. {#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

[^fn-constraint-auditing-c07]: **Timing constraint integrity and waiver auditing**: Automated design loops optimizing for timing slack face a subtle reward-hacking failure mode: relaxing constraints to falsely clear violations. Beyond crude `set_false_path` additions, an agent can subtly relax clock uncertainty, artificially increase maximum transition limits, alter on-chip variation derating tables, or declare optimistic multicycle path exceptions. Constraint files (SDC) must be cryptographically hashed and diff-audited against immutable baseline constraints, with all multicycle exceptions formally verified against pipeline hazard logic.

Public RTL regression logs show why these admission records must separate aggregate pass rates and testbench artifacts from hardware defects before any result steers search. In one retained OpenTitan Ibex nightly regression report [@LowRISCIbex2026OpenTitanRegression], `{python} s16_pass` of `{python} s16_total` test runs pass (`{python} s16_pct`%) across `{python} s16_groups` named test groups, yet `{python} s16_nonpass_groups` groups record failures, including `{python} s16_dbg_pass` of `{python} s16_dbg_tot` passing runs in `debug_triggers` and `{python} s16_ill_pass` of `{python} s16_ill_tot` in `illegal_instr`. Nor is a recorded regression failure automatically an RTL defect: across two regression reports attached to Ibex issue 2187 (`{python} s22_r1_fail` failures in `{python} s22_r1_tot` runs and `{python} s22_r2_fail` in `{python} s22_r2_tot` runs on a later commit and seed range) [@LowRISCIbex2024Issue2187], the issue author's `{python} s22_mapped_n` explicit case-to-signature mappings attribute `{python} s22_non_rtl_n` cases to random-instruction generator wall-clock timeouts, stale testbench privilege-mode checkers, co-simulation configuration, or transient host timeouts and only `{python} s22_rtl_n` to a low-concern RTL behavior.

Meeting all seven admission criteria makes a metric eligible for comparison, but does not by itself validate the comparison.[^fn-constraint-auditing-c07] Comparing two candidates requires evaluating the full experimental delta under matched operating conditions, as developed in @sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope. Even before comparing candidates, the architect must also distinguish an empirical measurement from a formal proof that a candidate obeys a required contract: a cache's measured average latency and a proof that its controller preserves transaction ordering answer different questions, even when both arrive through the same execution harness.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Consider a hypothetical return from evaluating a prospective L2 cache configuration for the Lighthouse XR subsystem under a 3\ W thermal design power envelope. Suppose static UPF checks pass, but a bounded model checking (BMC) run encounters a setup failure, and a thermal report omits raw trace lineage. These statuses illustrate routing; the Lighthouse study has not executed.

**Application.** For the thermal value, the required context includes the activity trace, power and thermal models, applicable operating conditions, and extraction procedure. Hardware and software revisions, the instruction set architecture (ISA), compiler state, and memory timing assumptions must also be identified where they affect that activity or its interpretation. The missing raw trace lineage prevents this value from entering a comparison; unrelated completed checks retain their own scope. Passing static UPF checks neither supplies that lineage nor resolves the BMC setup failure.

**Outcome.** The setup failure routes to environment repair, and the incomplete thermal value remains unqualified. Neither return establishes a defect in the architectural candidate. Retaining that distinction prevents infrastructure failures from becoming false negative training labels.
:::

## Formal Bounds and Sequential Equivalence {#sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence}

When an automated repair or retiming loop modifies pipeline control logic, dynamic simulation across sampled execution traces can easily miss a rare multi-master stall deadlock that requires a specific cycle-level interleaving to trigger. Catching such corner-case hazards before spending compute and licenses on downstream synthesis and place-and-route runs requires formal checks, which evaluate interface protocol compliance, control invariants, or circuit equivalence directly against a candidate's declared model and assumptions rather than against a matched performance baseline. Yet a clean exit from a formal solver is just as easy to misread as an unqualified simulator log. A solver that stops at a finite cycle depth or passes under over-constrained input assumptions reports no violations without proving the hardware safe. Whereas a completed unbounded proof establishes that an implementation satisfies an invariant across every reachable state within its assumptions, a bounded search or an inconclusive solver run supports a much narrower conclusion, making the returned proof status as important as the property itself.

### Interpreting Formal Proofs and Equivalence Checks {#sec-proof-statuses-equivalence}

Running a formal engine inside an automated design loop immediately raises two practical questions: if the solver returns a failing trace on a simplified model, does that trace expose a genuine RTL bug or an artifact of the abstraction, and if an optimizer retimes pipeline stages, how do we verify that the modified circuit still implements the same architectural behavior? On the first question, formal verification tools such as JasperGold and VC Formal evaluate microarchitectural contracts expressed as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)[^fn-sva-c07] under explicit assumptions that constrain legal input sequences, resets, and clock domains [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. When a tool checks a simplified abstract model to keep the state space tractable, counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) tests any returned failure trace against the concrete RTL: *spurious counterexamples* (artifacts of an over-approximated abstraction that cannot occur in actual hardware) trigger automatic model refinement, whereas *realizable counterexamples* expose genuine RTL defects or specification errors [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR].[^fn-cegar-c07]

[^fn-sva-c07]: **SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)**: A formal property specification language extending SystemVerilog with concurrent temporal logic constructs. Unlike instantaneous software assertions, concurrent SVA expressions evaluate multi-cycle temporal sequences (e.g., verifying that a valid request is followed by an acknowledge within three cycles) across clock edges, enabling both formal model checking and simulation coverage tracking.

[^fn-cegar-c07]: **CEGAR (Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement)**: A fundamental formal verification algorithm. To avoid state-space explosion, CEGAR starts by verifying a simplified (over-approximated) model of the hardware. If the solver finds a violating path, it checks whether that path is possible in the concrete model. A realizable path violates the encoded property under its assumptions; interpreting it as an RTL defect still requires the intended contract and model to agree. If the path is spurious, the abstraction is refined to exclude it and checking continues.

On the second question, completed formal proofs can establish behavioral equivalence across hardware representations after synthesis or microarchitectural edits. When register boundaries remain fixed, *combinational equivalence checking* (CEC) compares logic cones between aligned state elements to verify that logic synthesis preserves gate-level truth tables. When an optimization instead shifts pipeline register boundaries, retimes stages, or alters transaction latencies, *sequential equivalence checking* (SEC)[^fn-sec-cec-c07] verifies input-output correspondence across cycles, subject to the cycle correspondence defined for the check [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. At block interfaces, *assume-guarantee reasoning* decomposes system verification into modular contracts, proving, for example, that if a bus fabric preserves transaction ordering, the attached accelerator cannot overflow its credit queue [@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts].

[^fn-sec-cec-c07]: **Sequential vs. Combinational Equivalence (SEC vs. CEC)**: Combinational equivalence checking (CEC) compares logic between 1-to-1 mapped flip-flops, scaling efficiently for logic synthesis signoff. Sequential equivalence checking (SEC) verifies behavioral input-output equivalence when state elements are retimed, pipelined, or restructured. Because SEC requires exploring reachability across arbitrary state-transition graphs, it faces PSPACE-complete complexity and severe state-space explosion on complex microarchitectures.

Every equivalence check must define what counts as 'the same behavior' for the architectural claim at hand. Because CEC compares combinational functions under a fixed one-to-one state pairing while SEC reasons about behavior across cycles, an SEC setup must explicitly specify which retiming shifts or latency changes the specification allows. Without that allowance, a rigid cycle-by-cycle comparison will reject a candidate that legitimately changes interface timing, lengthens a tolerated latency, or reorders independent transactions within architectural rules, while replacing the reference model with the candidate itself would merely evade the check.

When an optimization alters cycle-by-cycle timing within those architectural rules, the required relationship is refinement: every behavior of the implementation must map to a behavior permitted by the specification through a *refinement mapping* that relates implementation states to specification states [@AbadiLamport1991RefinementMappings]. Because the verification setup must declare these permitted latency shifts and protocol correspondences up front, a log reporting 'equivalence passed' certifies only the specific reference model and correspondence that the tool actually checked.

### Bounded Search and Vacuity {#sec-bounded-search-vacuity}

When full state-space exploration is intractable, BMC unrolls the hardware transition relation to a finite depth $k$ to hunt for shallow defects [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Finding no counterexample through depth $k$ supports a bounded claim, but establishing unbounded safety requires more than simply increasing $k$: the checker must either prove that depth $k$ already reaches the diameter of the state space or complete a separate unbounded proof using $k$-induction or property-directed reachability (IC3/PDR) [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR].

Unrolling to a larger depth $k$ explores longer execution traces, yet it can quickly exhaust the solver budget because proof difficulty depends on the property structure, transition relation, environment assumptions, abstraction choice, and solver heuristics rather than on a block's name or gate count alone. The status returned by the solver therefore dictates whether the next step is to inspect a failure trace, record a finite bound, qualify a completed proof, or revise an inconclusive check (@fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth).

![**A formal return determines the claim and the next check.** This unscaled decision diagram separates a returned violation trace, a completed bounded check, a completed unbounded proof, and a resource-limited run. A trace needs reachability and realizability checks; a finite bound remains bounded unless a completeness argument or separate proof closes the obligation. Every status retains the property, model, and assumptions.](images/fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth){#fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth width="100%" fig-alt="Decision diagram routing a formal return to four outcomes. A violation trace requires reachability and realizability checks. A completed unbounded proof supports a scoped Proved status. A completed bounded check without a proof supports Bounded-only through k. An unfinished query is Inconclusive, with any completed bound qualified separately."}

When a solver times out or runs out of memory, the run establishes neither a hardware defect nor a proof; the verification plan must instead adjust the resource budget, refine the abstraction, or decompose the proof using modular contracts or inductive invariants. Any smaller bound $k$ that the solver completed before timing out can still be recorded, provided its depth and assumptions remain explicit, since additional elapsed solver time prior to a timeout adds no logical coverage beyond the last completed depth.

What a formal run must check also depends on the class of property being verified. *Safety properties* rule out forbidden states (such as two masters driving a bus simultaneously), whereas *liveness properties* require eventual progress (such as every request eventually receiving a grant), often under explicit fairness assumptions [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness]. Both safety and liveness are trace properties that can be evaluated on one execution trace at a time, even though a liveness counterexample requires a looping infinite trace. Security guarantees such as noninterference, by contrast, ask whether changing a secret input can alter what an unprivileged observer sees across executions. Because noninterference compares observations across multiple traces rather than inspecting a single trace in isolation, it is a *hyperproperty* [@ClarksonSchneider2010Hyperproperties].[^fn-hyper-c07] Although general hyperproperties can relate arbitrary sets of traces, hardware security tools often check two-trace observational equivalence: SPECTECTOR, for example, verifies speculative noninterference via symbolic execution under declared speculative semantics by comparing attacker observations with and without speculation [@GuarnieriEtAl2020SPECTECTOR]. Identifying the property class therefore fixes the structure of the verification query before unrolling depth and solver budgets are chosen.

[^fn-hyper-c07]: **Hyperproperties**: Hyperproperties describe relationships across multiple execution traces, such as constant-time execution in cryptography, where the required timing observations must not reveal differences in secrets when public inputs and relevant conditions are held fixed.

Even when a solver reports that a property holds, the check is meaningless if the property passed vacuously without exercising the hardware behavior it was meant to constrain [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity].[^fn-vacuity-antecedent-c07] An assertion that every accepted request eventually receives a response, for example, will pass trivially if an overly restrictive environment assumption prevents any request from ever being accepted. Pairing the assertion with a cover query for request acceptance under the exact same assumptions tests whether the trigger is actually reachable: finding a witness trace rules out antecedent vacuity (though it does not by itself prove the response obligation), whereas an unreachable trigger warns the verification team to fix the assumptions or trigger condition before claiming progress, and a bounded search that finds no witness leaves reachability beyond that depth open.

[^fn-vacuity-antecedent-c07]: **Vacuous assertion passes**: In formal logic, a conditional implication $A \implies B$ evaluates to true whenever the antecedent $A$ is false. In hardware assertion checking, if environment assumptions or upstream wiring permanently suppress an antecedent signal (such as a request handshake never asserting), the assertion passes with a nominal 100% formal score while leaving the required consequence $B$ completely unexercised. Formal signoff flows therefore commonly pair assertions with cover properties that show each antecedent can fire under the environment assumptions.

The risk of vacuous or malformed properties increases when assertions are drafted automatically. Evaluations of language-model assertion generators such as AssertLLM find a nontrivial share of syntactically invalid or semantically wrong assertions [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. Generated assertions therefore require syntactic and semantic qualification alongside seeded-mutant checks that test whether the assertion suite actually catches injected RTL bugs, since mutation testing measures fault sensitivity that antecedent reachability alone cannot establish (@sec-semantic-rtl-defects).

Once a safety assertion and its assumptions are qualified against vacuity, one standard way to lift a bounded check into an unbounded proof is $k$-induction, which extends ordinary mathematical induction to sequential circuits in two steps: first verify that no bug occurs within the first $k$ cycles from reset, and then prove that any trajectory that stays safe for $k+1$ consecutive cycles must remain safe on the next cycle as well. Formally, under the following indexing convention, the *base query* $B_k$ searches for a property violation from the initial state through step $k$, while the *inductive-step query* $S_k$ searches for a transition from states $s_0$ through $s_k$ that satisfy the property to a state $s_{k+1}$ that violates it:

$$B_k = \bigvee_{j=0}^{k}\left(Init(s_0) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{j-1} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_j)\right),$$

$$S_k = \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} P(s_i) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_{k+1}),$$

where $Init(s_0)$ constrains the initial state, $T(s_i, s_{i+1})$ is the hardware transition relation, and $P(s)$ is the target safety invariant. The base query checks every prefix length from zero through $k$, including traces that cannot continue (with the empty transition conjunction at $j=0$ taken as true). If $B_k$ is unsatisfiable, no violation is reachable from $Init$ through step $k$, provided $Init$ encodes the reset assumptions the claim requires. If $S_k$ is also unsatisfiable, no $k+1$ consecutive safe states $s_0,\ldots,s_k$ can step into a violating state $s_{k+1}$, and the two unsatisfiability results together establish unbounded safety for this induction construction; a satisfiable $B_k$, by contrast, returns a reachable counterexample trace.

Because the inductive-step query $S_k$ does not require its starting state $s_0$ to be reachable from $Init$, a trace that satisfies $S_k$ may begin in an unreachable state of the circuit, producing a *spurious inductive counterexample* rather than a real hardware bug. Rather than adding an unverified assumption that might accidentally mask a genuine defect, the verifier can increase the induction depth $k$ or prove auxiliary invariants $Inv(s)$ so that the strengthened invariant $P(s) \land Inv(s)$ holds from $Init$ and is preserved across transitions. Alternatively, the solver can switch to PDR/IC3, which maintains over-approximated reachability frames $F_0, F_1, \dots, F_k$ and learns blocking clauses until it converges on an inductive invariant or exposes a reachable violation [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR].

Whether a solver uses bounded unrolling, $k$-induction, or PDR/IC3, its returned status dictates which engineering action is valid next (@tbl-formal-result-status).

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proved** | Property holds for recorded model and assumptions under verified checking components. | Discharge the scoped architectural claim once the property and assumptions are qualified, including relevant vacuity checks. |
| **Counterexample** | A trace satisfies the violation query; its reachability and realizability depend on the query and abstraction. | Check reachability and realizability. Refine a spurious abstraction, strengthen a failed induction argument with proved invariants, or repair RTL or specification for a confirmed failure. |
| **Bounded-only** | No counterexample found through depth $k$. | Record finite bound; extend search, seek a completeness argument or separate proof, or leave unbounded safety open. |
| **Inconclusive** | Solver timed out or exceeded memory limits. | Revise abstraction, decompose assumptions, or adjust resource bounds. Never report as a pass. |
: **Formal result status dictates next technical actions in verification feedback.** Proofs discharge scoped claims; counterexamples and bounds drive targeted repairs or open records. {#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Keeping these four statuses distinct prevents two common reporting errors. An inconclusive run establishes neither a proof nor a violation, even if the solver completed a shallower bound that can be qualified separately, because a clean process exit never substitutes for a proved property. A bounded-only return carries the opposite temptation: it provides real evidence through depth $k$, so that bound $k$ must travel with the record wherever it is cited, lest a finite check quietly be read as an unbounded guarantee.

## Dynamic Coverage and Mutation Testing {#sec-semantic-rtl-defects}

Even a complete formal proof covers only what its property set, model, and assumptions name (@sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence); claims outside that scope still need other checks. Full system-on-chip software workloads and dynamic thermal behavior exceed the modeling and scale limits of formal analysis, whereas cycle-accurate simulation and hardware emulation can exercise long execution traces without covering every corner case. Verification suites therefore combine both approaches, using formal proofs for selected interface protocols, arbiters, and crossing properties while relying on dynamic evaluation to measure workload throughput, power, and end-to-end latency under the modeled conditions.

In practice, dynamic verification pairs constrained-random simulation (Synopsys VCS, Verilator) and Universal Verification Methodology (UVM)[^fn-uvm-c07] coverage metrics [@IEEE2020UVM; @IEEE2023SystemVerilog] with hardware emulation platforms (Palladium, ZeBu, Veloce), while low-power verification combines static Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 UPF power-state tables with low-power-aware simulation to verify power isolation clamping cells and level shifters across power domains [@IEEE2024UPF]. Because an RTL simulation that omits power-state transitions leaves their effects untested, any power estimate also depends on qualifying the transitions that actually ran.

[^fn-uvm-c07]: **Universal Verification Methodology (UVM / IEEE 1800.2)**: A standardized SystemVerilog class library for building modular, transaction-level verification testbenches. UVM structures environments into reusable stimulus generators, drivers, monitors, and scoreboards, combining constrained-random stimulus generation with functional coverage metrics to test complex protocols.

Even when those transitions and workloads are exercised, however, sampled dynamic simulation cannot prove the absence of rare corner-case bugs, as demonstrated by the historic Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) lookup table defect [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Colwell2006PentiumChronicles]. That flaw involved five incorrect entries in the radix-4 Sweeney-Robertson-Tocher (SRT) division lookup table, which Intel estimated corrupted about one in 9 billion random divisions [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision]; Intel later turned to formal verification to validate the Core i7 execution engine [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV flaw and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** The Pentium floating-point divider had passed its pre-silicon verification and shipped.

**The gap.** Five entries in its SRT division lookup table were incorrect, and pre-silicon verification did not expose the defect. A defect that corrupts about one random division in 9 billion is almost invisible to sampled simulation.

**The lesson.** Sampled dynamic simulation cannot establish the absence of a defect in a large input space. A claim of absence needs a check that covers the space, which is why formal verification later took on execution-engine validation.
:::

Sampled stimulus is only one limit of dynamic coverage; the checker itself is the other. A testbench drafted alongside the RTL can execute defective logic without flagging the wrong outcome, especially when both inherit the same omitted requirement. Because clean syntax and elaboration leave semantic and physical questions open across clock and reset crossings, interface ordering, and power-domain isolation, the following eight examples show which checks can catch each class of defect, without claiming an empirical ranking of how often they occur in generated RTL.

1. **Inferred latches and combinational loops.** An incomplete assignment in intended combinational logic can imply state retention, producing a latch inference[^fn-inferred-latches-c07] or a tool diagnostic. Because functional tests establish only the behaviors their stimulus happens to exercise, they can miss both the unintended behavior and the timing obligations a latch introduces, such as hold checks;[^fn-hold-timing-c07] lint and synthesis reports expose unintended storage and combinational feedback directly.
2. **Clock-domain crossing (CDC) and reset-domain crossing (RDC) metastability.**[^fn-cdc-c07] An asynchronous input that changes near a receiving clock edge can leave a flip-flop metastable, risking an unsettled output when downstream logic samples it. Synchronization must therefore fit the transfer: a dual-rank synchronizer can reduce that risk for a suitable single-bit control signal, whereas a multi-bit transfer needs a coherence-preserving protocol such as a properly designed asynchronous first-in, first-out buffer, and reset deassertion that violates recovery or removal timing can likewise leave state elements inconsistent. Because ordinary RTL simulation does not model the analog settling process, dedicated CDC and RDC analysis checks crossing structures, protocols, and assumptions, supplemented by formal or metastability-injection checks where appropriate.
3. **Interface handshake and memory-ordering violations.** An Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) source that waits for `READY` before asserting `VALID` can deadlock with a receiver waiting for `VALID`, and dropping an unacknowledged transfer can lose data, yet a testbench whose receiver never stalls may miss both defects. Interface assertions and assume-guarantee proofs check those handshake obligations directly. A separate coverage gap arises in memory ordering: generated logic or software that assumes sequential consistency can fail under behaviors permitted by RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO),[^fn-rvwmo-c07] so memory-model tests or proofs must exercise those behaviors and compare them against the declared memory model rather than relying on core count alone.
4. **Bitwidth truncation and overflow.** A vector accumulator that silently drops precision can pass stimulus that never reaches the affected range. Width lint flags potential truncation, while directed boundary-value tests or formal checks establish whether the implemented wraparound or saturation matches the specification.
5. **Unhandled reset states in finite state machines (FSMs).** An FSM lacking a recovery transition from an unused encoding can become stuck if a fault or unexpected control sequence places it there. FSM lint and reachability analysis help identify missing recovery paths, whereas simulation detects the problem only when its stimulus and fault model exercise that state, and any fault-injection claim also needs a model of how the fault enters the machine.
6. **Four-state $1\text{'bx}$ optimism.** Under ordinary IEEE 1800 semantics, `if (1'bx)` takes the `else` branch [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog], which can hide uncertainty about an uninitialized or otherwise unknown control value. Because X is a simulation value rather than a particular physical voltage, the corresponding hardware may hold either logic value or suffer from a different electrical problem.[^fn-x-optimism-c07] X-propagation-aware simulation and formal checks that account for unknown initial states expose behaviors masked by standard branch semantics while keeping their unknown-value assumptions explicit.
7. **Missing isolation and level shifting across power domains.** Crossing between power domains requires level shifting when domain voltages are incompatible and isolation when a powered-down domain could drive an active receiver [@IEEE2024UPF]. Omitting required isolation can feed an invalid logic level into an active domain, where an input in the range $V_{tn} < V_{in} < V_{dd} - |V_{tp}|$ in a simplified CMOS inverter can turn on both transistor networks at once and draw crowbar current. Static UPF checks and low-power-aware simulation verify the declared structure and modeled behavior, but they do not quantify all electrical consequences, including latchup risk,[^fn-latchup-c07] which require dedicated device and power-network analysis.
8. **Silent false paths and multicycle overrides in SDC constraints.** When an optimizer hides a real timing violation by inserting an unjustified `set_false_path` or `set_multicycle_path` directive, static timing analysis produces a clean report because the timing engine trusts the supplied constraints, as illustrated by the hypothetical 850\ ps case in @sec-timing-exception-attacks that reports no negative slack despite a real setup failure. Catching an invalid exception therefore requires independent constraint review and SDC lint alongside the timing report.

[^fn-inferred-latches-c07]: **Inferred Latches**: Intended combinational logic must define each output under every relevant input condition. An incomplete assignment that requires retention of the previous value can infer a level-sensitive latch, unless the logic is optimized away or rejected by the tool. Intentional latch-based circuits are valid designs, but unintended latches introduce timing, race-avoidance, and test obligations that the original combinational design may not address.

[^fn-hold-timing-c07]: **Hold Timing**: A timing constraint requiring data to remain stable at a flip-flop's input for a minimum duration after the active clock edge. A violation can cause incorrect capture or metastability. Lowering the clock frequency generally does not repair a same-edge hold violation, because its requirement depends on the relative clock and data arrival times rather than the clock period; data-path delay or clock-skew repair may be needed.

[^fn-cdc-c07]: **CDC/RDC Metastability**: A clock or reset crossing can violate a receiving element's timing requirements and create a risk of metastability or inconsistent state. Synchronization and crossing protocols reduce that risk under declared assumptions; a digital simulation without a metastability model does not measure the analog settling behavior.

[^fn-rvwmo-c07]: **RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO)**: The RISC-V memory consistency model permits reorderings not forbidden by its preserved program order and memory-model axioms. Ordering constraints include applicable fences, acquire/release annotations, and specified address, data, control, and pipeline dependencies [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. Tests restricted to sequentially consistent behavior cannot expose failures that require permitted weak-memory outcomes; the exercised behaviors and checker determine the coverage.

[^fn-x-optimism-c07]: **Four-State Logic and X-Optimism**: Four-state simulation distinguishes 0, 1, Z (high impedance), and X (unknown). For the single-bit condition `if (1'bx)`, ordinary SystemVerilog semantics select the `else` branch, potentially masking uncertainty [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. X can represent uninitialized state, conflicting drivers, or another unknown modeled value. It does not identify a particular physical voltage or establish metastability.

[^fn-latchup-c07]: **Latchup**: A destructive condition in CMOS circuits where parasitic bipolar transistors form a low-impedance path between power and ground rails, causing excessive current flow that can permanently damage the silicon unless power is removed.

That blind spot widens when the same large language model (LLM) family generates both the RTL and its testbench, because both artifacts can reproduce the same omitted requirement in a *self-verification paradox*. Mutation testing challenges the verification suite by introducing synthetic faults (such as inverted branch conditions, altered arithmetic operators, or stuck-at registers) and measuring which non-equivalent mutants[^fn-equivalent-mutants-c07] the testbench detects.[^fn-red-teaming-c07] Whereas structural coverage records only which code lines or state transitions ran, mutation analysis directly tests whether the suite observes incorrect behavior when faults occur. In RISC-V compliance testing, for example, mutants seeded into a reference instruction-set simulator survived the official test suite and exposed classes of implementation error that the suite never checked [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance].

[^fn-equivalent-mutants-c07]: **Equivalent mutants**: Syntactically modified circuit variants that retain identical input-output behavior to the golden design across all reachable states (such as dead-code changes or don't-care condition rewrites). Because no test vector can detect an equivalent mutant, identifying and filtering them via formal equivalence checks prevents artificially depressed mutation kill scores.

[^fn-red-teaming-c07]: **The ML safety parallel**: Reward hacking occurs when an optimizer obtains a high score through behavior the intended task should not reward [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete]. The hardware analogue is a candidate exploiting a proxy or testbench omission. Generating a testbench alongside the RTL can reproduce that omission; adversarial tests instead challenge the agreement by asking whether the harness detects deliberately introduced faults. This analogy motivates a check of the evaluator, not a claim that the two research problems have identical causes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Inline values for the CV32E40P and mutation-analysis paragraphs and
# @fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities, read from the same transcribed
# datasets the figure plots:
#   data/datasets/chapter7-defect-discovery-modalities.csv
#     (OpenHW CV32E40P User Manual, Verification, Tables 9 and 10)
#   data/datasets/chapter7-herdt-mutation-compliance.csv
#     (Herdt et al., ASP-DAC 2021, Table 1)
import csv as _csv7
import re as _re7
from pathlib import Path as _Path7
import _python.plots as _ap7

_root7 = _Path7(_ap7.__file__).resolve().parents[2]


class _Raw7:
    """Render inline without quotes, so Quarto emits the text unescaped."""

    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text

    def __repr__(self):
        return self.text


def _rows7(name):
    with open(_root7 / "data" / "datasets" / name, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        return list(_csv7.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))


_mod7 = {r["modality"]: int(r["issues_found"]) for r in _rows7("chapter7-defect-discovery-modalities.csv")}
_grp7 = {}
for _r in _rows7("chapter7-defect-discovery-modalities.csv"):
    _grp7[_r["method_group"]] = _grp7.get(_r["method_group"], 0) + int(_r["issues_found"])
cv_total = sum(_mod7.values())
cv_sim = _grp7["simulation"]
cv_nonsim = _grp7["non-simulation"]
cv_directed = _mod7["Simulation: directed, self-checking test"]
cv_step = _mod7["Simulation: step-and-compare with ISS"]
cv_random = _mod7["Simulation: constrained-random"]
cv_formal = _mod7["Formal verification"]
cv_inspect = _mod7["Inspection (human review)"]
cv_lint = _mod7["Lint"]
cv_nonsim_pct = round(100 * cv_nonsim / cv_total, 1)
# The prose states these relations in words ("13 each", "one has no recorded source").
assert cv_formal == cv_inspect
assert _grp7["unknown"] == 1

_mut7 = {int(r["stage_order"]): r for r in _rows7("chapter7-herdt-mutation-compliance.csv")}
mut_seeded = _Raw7(f"{int(_mut7[1]['mutants_entering']):,}")
mut_official_killed = _Raw7(f"{int(_mut7[1]['mutants_killed']):,}")
mut_official_pct = round(100 * int(_mut7[1]["mutants_killed"]) / int(_mut7[1]["mutants_entering"]), 1)
mut_survivors = int(_mut7[1]["mutants_surviving"])
_spec_n7 = int(_re7.search(r"\d+", _mut7[2]["tests_description"]).group())
mut_spec_tests = _Raw7(f"{_spec_n7:,}")
mut_spec_killed = int(_mut7[2]["mutants_killed"])
mut_symbolic_tests = int(_mut7[3]["mutants_killed"])
# The prose says symbolic execution "killed the remainder".
assert int(_mut7[3]["mutants_surviving"]) == 0
assert int(_mut7[2]["mutants_entering"]) == mut_survivors
```

Published verification records show why a verification suite needs both diverse checkers and direct fault-detection tests (@fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities). When the OpenHW Group identified and resolved `{python} cv_total` RTL issues in its CV32E40P RISC-V core between the start of verification in February 2020 and RTL freeze, it recorded the method that found each one [@OpenHW2026CV32E40PManual]. Simulation found `{python} cv_sim` of those issues (`{python} cv_directed` through directed self-checking tests, `{python} cv_step` through step-and-compare against an instruction-set simulator, and `{python} cv_random` through constrained-random stimulus), whereas formal verification and human inspection found `{python} cv_formal` each, lint found `{python} cv_lint`, and one has no recorded source. Methods other than simulation therefore account for `{python} cv_nonsim` of the `{python} cv_total` issues ($`{python} cv_nonsim_pct`\%$). Although these counts come from one core's campaign without reporting the effort, compute, execution ordering, or overlapping coverage needed to rank the methods by efficiency or determine which other checks could have caught each defect, they show that no single method was credited with finding all the issues in the campaign.

The second panel of @fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities turns from the design to the test suite itself. When @HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance seeded `{python} mut_seeded` single mutations across nine mutation classes into a reference RISC-V instruction-set simulator, the official compliance suite killed `{python} mut_official_killed` of them ($`{python} mut_official_pct`\%$); a specification-based suite of about `{python} mut_spec_tests` further tests then killed `{python} mut_spec_killed` of the `{python} mut_survivors` survivors, and symbolic execution generated `{python} mut_symbolic_tests` targeted tests that killed the remainder. Because those surviving mutants included shift instructions that used unmasked upper bits of the shift-amount register and jumps that wrote the destination register even when a misaligned target should have trapped without side effects, they show that a suite that every conforming simulator passes can still fail to distinguish faulty ones.

![**Different checks find different defects, and a passing suite can leave detectable faults alive.** (a) Method that found each of the `{python} cv_total` RTL issues resolved before CV32E40P RTL freeze; non-simulation methods account for `{python} cv_nonsim` [@OpenHW2026CV32E40PManual]. (b) Mutants seeded into a reference RISC-V instruction-set simulator, with each suite run on the previous suite's survivors; the official compliance tests leave `{python} mut_survivors` of `{python} mut_seeded` alive [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance].](images/fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities){#fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel bar chart. The left panel counts the 47 CV32E40P RTL issues by the method that found them, with formal verification and inspection at 13 each, directed simulation 10, step-and-compare 6, constrained-random simulation 2, lint 2, and one unknown. The right panel shows three test suites applied in turn to seeded simulator mutants, killing 2,263 of 2,455, then 91 of 192, then all remaining 101."}

The same mutation loop can guide automated property and test generation, a use of automation that this book proposes though it is not yet evaluated here. Rather than mutating flattened post-synthesis gate netlists, where logic minimization and technology mapping destroy high-level signal semantics and create synthetic nets, the environment injects mutations directly at the source RTL abstract syntax tree (AST) level by modifying conditional branches, operator polarities, or state transitions. After a bounded formal equivalence budget filters out equivalent mutants, the simulation suite runs against the remaining faults. Whenever a mutant survives, the environment returns the mutation details and source context to a model that proposes an SVA property or a directed testbench sequence, and rerunning the suite establishes whether the new check detects the fault while accepting the correct design. Killing the retained mutants supports a claim about detecting that tested fault set, though it still does not establish that all corner cases have been found, that the original specification is complete, or that the generator and checker have no shared omissions.

Shared omissions are especially likely when an evaluator comes from the same model family as the generator, because such a second opinion can corroborate an answer without independently challenging it, the distinction developed in @fig-independent-checks and treated as a red-team target in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. A design environment therefore needs fault-detection measurements alongside structural coverage, together with claim-specific checks whose assumptions and limits remain visible. Both formal proofs and dynamic test suites still depend on the specification they are given, and passing those functional checks is only the prerequisite for comparing candidates on performance, power, and area.

## Scoping a Comparison to the Claim It Supports {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

Once a candidate satisfies its functional checks and its individual measurements meet the admission criteria, an empirical claim that one design outperforms a baseline requires a controlled evaluation that separates the hardware effect from confounding variation across compiler lowering, initial memory states, cache warmup intervals, simulator versions, and operating corners [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Without those controls, an isolated delta cannot distinguish a hardware gain from simulation jitter, cold-start cache artifacts, or compiler phase-ordering shifts. Every comparison therefore binds the candidate and comparator revisions to a measured difference and an uncertainty model under explicit operating conditions (@fig-claim-frame).

![**Comparative claim frames bind candidate and baseline designs to measured deltas.** Compared designs (candidate and comparator) map to measured results (quantities, units, differences, and uncertainty). These remain conditional on experimental scope (workloads, architectural state, tool versions, PVT corners, and check nonclaims). A change in evaluation scope creates a distinct comparison rather than an interchangeable measurement.](images/fig-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame width="80%" fig-alt="Three-column diagram of a comparison frame. Candidate and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty. These are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

For a matched set of architectural evaluation cases $c_j \in \mathcal{C}$ (representing identical benchmark inputs, initial cache states, and PVT operating corners), the paired difference is:

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j),
$$

where $y(\cdot)$ denotes the evaluated architectural metric. For positive per-benchmark performance ratios, a geometric mean preserves comparisons when the normalization reference changes, provided the benchmark set and weights remain fixed [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]; if the claim concerns total execution time for a specified workload mix, the evaluation should instead aggregate execution times using that mix before forming a ratio.

Even when benchmark inputs and tool versions are held fixed, run-to-run variation and phase behavior require an uncertainty interval around the paired differences. For paired observations with temporal dependence, block resampling[^fn-block-bootstrap-c07] estimates uncertainty while preserving local dependence within sampled blocks [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap], with the block choice and sampling assumptions remaining part of the interval's qualification. Before running the comparison, we also declare a practical decision margin $m$, the smallest difference in $y$ that would justify changing the architecture. Comparing the confidence interval against zero and $\pm m$ then separates three outcomes: if the interval crosses zero, the direction of the effect remains unresolved; if it lies wholly inside $[-m, +m]$, the difference is too small to change the decision even if its sign is clear, and the result is retained under @tbl-feedback-destinations without forcing a design update.

[^fn-block-bootstrap-c07]: **Block Bootstrapping**: A non-parametric resampling technique designed for time-series data with temporal dependence. In computer systems, performance metrics like instructions per cycle and memory latency cluster into execution phases. Independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$) resampling discards this temporal structure and can misestimate variance, commonly understating it when observations are positively correlated. Block bootstrapping resamples contiguous chunks to retain local dependence; its validity still depends on the process and block-selection assumptions.

Claiming a decision-relevant improvement requires the third outcome, in which the confidence interval clears $m$ entirely in the metric's favorable direction. Taking differences as candidate minus comparator, the interval must lie wholly below $-m$ for a lower-is-better metric such as latency, or wholly above $+m$ for a higher-is-better metric such as throughput. When an interval excludes zero but still straddles the favorable threshold $\pm m$, the data support the direction of the gain without resolving whether it is large enough to justify the change; further measurement is warranted only if resolving that ambiguity could alter the architectural decision.

A single paired comparison is still not enough when an optimizer selects the top performer from thousands of noisy evaluations. Because choosing the best observed score introduces the selection bias that @sec-support-limits named the optimizer's curse,[^fn-winners-curse-c07] the estimates used to pick a winner tend to overstate its advantage, and the apparent margin requires an independent confirmatory measurement before it can support an improvement claim.

[^fn-winners-curse-c07]: **Winner's Curse**: Selection among noisy estimates can overstate the selected candidate's value. Independent confirmation addresses that selected result; multiple-comparison procedures address related inference problems under their own assumptions and do not repair systematic model error.

::: {.callout-law title="The Winner's Curse in Candidate Optimization Sweeps"}
**The Classical Principle:** Selecting the top performer from a set of noisy estimates systematically favors optimistic error, a hazard that the winner's curse names in competitive bidding [@CapenEtAl1971CompetitiveBidding; @Thaler1988WinnersCurse] and that the optimizer's curse generalizes to decision analysis [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. For a fixed finite candidate set in which candidate $i$ has true value $v_i$ (with larger values preferred) and unbiased estimate $\hat v_i$, selecting $I=\arg\max_i\hat v_i$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\hat v_I-v_I]\geq0$ across repeated evaluations. That inequality is strict whenever noise can cause a suboptimal candidate to be selected, although it describes an average selection effect rather than a guarantee that every winning estimate is too high or has the largest measurement error.

**The Hardware Trap:** A sweep can select a microarchitecture partly because a sampled workload phase or random tool variation favored it. A deterministic simulator omission presents a distinct hazard, because repeated runs with the same model will reproduce the same misleading advantage.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Confirm the selected design on fresh seeds where randomness matters and on held-out workload phases. Challenge suspected model omissions with a check that can observe them, because reseeding the same simulator cannot expose a deterministic blind spot (@sec-law-winners-curse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Qualifying Proxies and Calibration {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

Independent confirmatory evaluation tests a selected candidate, but exploration also needs fast analytical cost models, cycle-approximate simulators, and learned surrogates to decide which candidates are worth running through slower reference tools. When a fast surrogate diverges from physical behavior, search can exploit modeling omissions such as ignored dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bank serialization, interconnect contention, or thermal dissipation limits to improve the proxy score without improving the implementable hardware, a failure mode introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology as microarchitectural proxy gaming [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. Qualifying the proxy therefore requires separating *observed qualification strata*, regions represented by paired proxy and reference measurements, from *unsampled evaluation gaps* where the proxy extrapolates [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Reference observations establish where agreement can be assessed at all, while held-out checks within those strata establish whether that agreement is adequate for the intended decision (@fig-trust-calibration).

![**Proxy use requires both relevant observations and adequate agreement.** An unscaled workflow links candidate scope to matched proxy/reference observations, held-out diagnostics, and a bounded use decision. Missing observations or inadequate agreement call for further reference evaluation, proxy revision, or a deferred decision. A change in workload, tool, or operating conditions reopens qualification.](images/fig-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%" fig-alt="Flow diagram from candidate and intended proxy use to matched reference observations, held-out diagnostics, and use within the assessed scope. Missing evidence or inadequate agreement routes to reference evaluation, proxy revision, or deferral. Changed conditions reopen qualification."}

Once search enters an unsampled region, existing observations no longer justify the surrogate's reported error bounds, even if those bounds remain narrow. Neither a confident score nor calibration data elsewhere settles whether agreement holds in the new regime; matched reference measurements in that region must test whether the proxy's estimates and rankings remain useful for the declared use under the assessed conditions.

Because extrapolation into unsampled regions is only one way an evaluation can mislead search, the verification loop must audit the proxy and comparison setup across six distinct concerns, each requiring its own diagnostic check (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare proxy with stronger reference measurement on matched cases against the tolerance required for the intended use. | Disagreement beyond that tolerance leaves the intended use unsupported; other uses require separate checks. |
| **Observed coverage** | Map candidate and tool dimensions; identify unsampled gaps. | Evidence does not qualify candidates outside sampled strata. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error and ranking stability against decision margins on held-out cases. | Excessive error limits quantitative estimates; unstable rankings limit ordering for the declared use, even within observed strata. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed using matched contrasts. | Measured difference does not identify proposed architectural cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows and report dispersion. | If uncertainty prevents resolving the declared decision margin, the point estimate alone cannot justify the decision. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate selected candidate on fresh, unseen cases. | Original apparent margin is not independently confirmed. |
: **Each weakness requires a distinct diagnostic.** Adverse results eliminate specific inferences without making other diagnoses interchangeable. {#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

As the third column of @tbl-proxy-diagnostics emphasizes, each diagnostic limits what the architect can infer rather than certifying the proxy for every task. While failure on one task need not make the surrogate useless everywhere, any other use still requires its own qualification: a proxy that is too noisy for fine ranking might still support coarse screening if its false-acceptance and false-rejection behavior is acceptable for that screen, and passing checks within observed strata never establishes behavior outside their qualified scope. Even when individual metrics are qualified, moreover, comparing candidates across performance, power, and area requires an explicit multi-objective decision rule. Pareto dominance identifies when one candidate is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in at least one, whereas a scalar objective collapses multiple dimensions into particular preferences or tradeoffs that must be declared upfront [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

```{python}
#| echo: false

```

**Case study: scalar compression and masked write traffic.** In our retained study of systolic array aspect ratios under SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3], compressing multi-dimensional behavior into a single figure of merit hid a large difference in memory traffic. The $32 \times 32$ baseline and a $16 \times 64$ candidate returned an identical sum of reported cycles excluding prefetch (`{python} sa_cycles` cycles, taken from the report's `Total Cycles` column rather than `Total Cycles (incl. prefetch)` and therefore distinct from full workload elapsed time) and an identical unweighted mean of the three layers' reported overall utilization (`{python} sa_util_pct`%). Under the preregistered scalar score ($S = C_{\text{excl. prefetch}}/\bar{U}_{\text{frac}} = `{python} sa_score`$), the two designs tied.

A quantity that the scalar score omits separates them (@fig-proxy-mismatch). The $16 \times 64$ candidate reported `{python} sa_writes_wide` modeled DRAM-word writes against `{python} sa_writes_base` for the baseline, twice as many. Across these two retained SCALE-Sim quantities, the baseline dominates the candidate, delivering equal reported cycles excluding prefetch with half the modeled writes, whereas a scalar evaluator that omits write traffic treats the two designs as interchangeable. Because SCALE-Sim write counts are modeled quantities rather than measured physical bus traffic, this run alone cannot answer whether the extra writes would degrade wall-clock timing, energy, or thermals through bus contention; @sec-cross-stack-pattern-transfer bounds the energy question with a labeled derived estimate.

The study itself did not fall into this trap because it recommended retaining the $32 \times 32$ baseline when no candidate beat it by the preregistered 1\ percent margin, and the write difference was noticed only after the run. For automated exploration, however, the hazard is prospective: a search that sweeps aspect ratios $\theta \in \Theta$ inside a fixed template and ranks candidates solely by $S$ has no basis for preferring the baseline over the $16 \times 64$ candidate, and a tie-breaking rule could just as easily select the design with twice the modeled writes. Preventing that blind spot requires declaring every decision-relevant quantity, here write traffic alongside cycles, as an explicit objective or constraint before the search runs so that it shapes exploration rather than surfacing afterward. We return to this broader pattern, in which optimizing a single scalar hides a regression in an omitted dimension, as the Whac-a-Mole regression effect (@sec-law-whac-a-mole in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
