## Outcome, Mechanism, and Counterfactual Reasoning {#sec-outcome-mechanism-counterfactual}

A proxy qualified for a particular use in @sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration does not by itself explain why a candidate performs better. An observed top-line *outcome* and its proposed explanatory *mechanism* require separate judgments (@tbl-outcome-mechanism). When an automated optimizer modifies a microarchitectural feature, recording an improvement in top-line latency or throughput does not prove that the intended mechanism produced the gain. For instance, a cache-resizing candidate might post faster frame rendering times not because larger static random-access memory (SRAM) capacity reduced conflict misses, but because incidental compiler instruction alignment masked a memory-bus serialization stall. To show that the mechanism caused the gain, the architect needs counterfactual tests that hold confounding compiler, memory, and operating variables fixed while varying only the mechanism under test.

| **Evaluation question** | **Possible qualified status** | **Why the distinction matters** |
| - | - | - |
| **Did requested quantity change in declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved. | Latency confidence interval spanning zero leaves improvement unresolved. |
| **Did proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or untested. | Qualified reduction in capacity misses confirms bounded cache effect. |
| **Did intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by distinguishing contrast under identification assumptions. | Lower miss count alone does not prove it caused tail-latency reduction. |
| **What did the check fundamentally not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | Cache-local results do not establish thermal stability or functional correctness. |
: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results.** Intermediate effects cannot substitute for unresolved architectural comparisons. {#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[34,30,36]"}

Generated explanations need the same scrutiny. A fluent causal story about why a candidate succeeded remains a hypothesis until measurements test it. Useful observations include performance-counter deltas, cycle-accurate stall breakdowns, queue-occupancy profiles, and ablation traces in which the mechanism is switched off and the outcome remeasured.

In the cache example above, an architect can separate the two explanations by comparing the original and enlarged cache across two controlled instruction alignments on the same workload, holding all other compiler, memory, and operating settings fixed. If changing alignment reproduces the gain while adding capacity at a fixed alignment yields no resolved benefit, the test challenges the capacity explanation; if adding capacity improves latency at both alignments, the test supports a capacity contribution. Because both factors may act at once, an alignment gain does not by itself rule out a capacity effect: miss counts and bus-stall breakdowns help test the causal chain from larger capacity through fewer misses to lower latency, while any interaction between capacity and alignment belongs in the explanation rather than attributing the gain to capacity alone. Even then, the contrast supports a causal interpretation only insofar as the intervention changes the intended factor and all other relevant conditions remain matched.

The prospective Lighthouse L2 cache configuration shows what such a test has to separate. Enlarging the L2 cache might cut off-chip DRAM traffic enough to improve 99th-percentile frame latency, yet evaluating that benefit also requires counting added SRAM area, leakage, tag-array lookup delay, and network-on-chip (NoC) queue pressure. The same capacity increase that raises the hit rate can lengthen tag lookups or serialize NoC packets and make tail latency worse. Queue-occupancy profiles and latency distributions help distinguish a genuine capacity benefit from a queuing bottleneck in a way that a hit-rate delta on its own cannot.

Because these Lighthouse trade-offs are hypotheses rather than measured results, the telemetry also needs checks for simulator artifacts. A fixed-latency queueing model, omitted DRAM refresh cycles, or an unconstrained register-file assumption in the compiler backend can each manufacture an apparent mechanism that exists only inside the model. Even on real hardware, paired profiler counters show why a single intermediate metric such as warp occupancy cannot serve as a universal causal story for kernel speedups (@fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual).

![**Faster retained GPU kernels do not move intermediate profiler counters in one uniform direction.** Paired Round 1 (open circles) and fastest retained round (filled squares) across `{python} ka11_n` KernelBench tasks profiled with NVIDIA Nsight Compute in the KernelAgent artifacts [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts]: (a) kernel execution time relative to Round 1, (b) achieved warp occupancy, and (c) sustained DRAM throughput. In MaxPool 3D and 3D transposed convolution, the fastest retained kernel achieves lower execution time alongside *lower* achieved occupancy, whereas in matrix–vector multiplication both occupancy and DRAM throughput rise steeply.](images/fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual){#fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual width="100%" fig-alt="Three-panel dumbbell chart comparing Round 1 and the fastest retained optimization round across five KernelBench tasks on relative kernel time, achieved occupancy, and DRAM throughput. Latency drops or holds nearly steady across all five tasks, while occupancy rises sharply for matrix-vector multiplication but falls for MaxPool 3D and transposed 3D convolution."}

Across those `{python} ka11_n` paired Nsight Compute profiles [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts], matrix–vector multiplication lowers execution time from `{python} ka11_mv_t1`\ ms to `{python} ka11_mv_tb`\ ms while raising achieved warp occupancy from `{python} ka11_mv_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_mv_occb`% and DRAM throughput from `{python} ka11_mv_dram1`% to `{python} ka11_mv_dramb`%. In MaxPool 3D, by contrast, the fastest retained round cuts execution time from `{python} ka11_mp_t1`\ ms to `{python} ka11_mp_tb`\ ms (`{python} ka11_mp_rel` of Round 1 time) while achieved occupancy *falls* from `{python} ka11_mp_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_mp_occb`% and DRAM throughput rises from `{python} ka11_mp_dram1`% to `{python} ka11_mp_dramb`%; in 3D transposed convolution, occupancy similarly drops from `{python} ka11_tc_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_tc_occb`% as latency nearly halves. A post-hoc narrative that attributes every kernel speedup to higher warp occupancy would be contradicted by two of the five tasks, yet these paired endpoint profiles still observe co-movement across distinct kernel implementations rather than isolating a single mechanism. Even when controlled contrasts and model checks support a proposed mechanism, that conclusion remains scoped to the model and its identification assumptions. Otherwise, the mechanism remains contradicted, unresolved, or untested according to the evidence in @tbl-outcome-mechanism, even when a supported top-line outcome can still be retained separately.

## Combining Independent Checks to Catch Blind Spots {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

Testing whether an individual outcome or mechanism holds still leaves a broader risk: a candidate can pass functional simulation, prove a bus-interface assertion, and close setup timing at a nominal operating point, yet still fail on silicon when simultaneous vector-unit switching triggers a dynamic voltage droop that none of those checks modeled. Because passing any single check supports only the obligations that check actually observes, the architect must verify that the qualified results together cover every requirement of the design. Assurance engineering structures this argument by linking high-level performance, correctness, and physical claims to their supporting checks and explicit assumptions [@Kelly2004GSN].

For each requirement across physical limits, functional contracts, and quality-of-service bounds, the architect identifies the relevant checks, the conditions under which their results apply, and any remaining gap. Even when passing a check cannot establish a claim in full, a check capable of falsifying the claim remains a useful filter as long as the unexamined obligations are assigned elsewhere.

### Mapping Requirements to Verification Toolchains {#sec-mapping-requirements-toolchains}

Physical signoff requirements cannot be discharged at a single operating point because different failure mechanisms peak under conflicting silicon conditions: the slow-silicon corner that limits setup timing is not the fast-silicon corner that exposes hold violations or peak leakage, while dynamic IR-drop and electromigration depend on switching activity and current density.[^fn-em-c07] A compute subsystem that passes one physical check at a nominal point estimate can therefore fail severely under another corner or analysis engine. Covering the full operating envelope requires matching each physical requirement to both the tool and the conditions that stress it: static timing engines such as Cadence Tempus check setup and hold timing across specified modes and corners [@Cadence2021Tempus], power-integrity analysis such as RedHawk-SC addresses voltage drop and electromigration limits, and physical verification such as Calibre checks layout against the applicable rule deck. The verification plan must therefore name the relevant PVT conditions, activity assumptions, extraction models, and rules for each check, since neither a nominal point estimate nor a functional testbench establishes physical feasibility outside those declared conditions.

[^fn-em-c07]: **Electromigration (EM)**: The gradual displacement of metal atoms in a conductor caused by high current densities over time. This atomic movement leads to wire thinning and eventual open circuits, degrading chip reliability.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Architectural requirements remain unresolved for distinct structural reasons"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse compute subsystem requirements span physical constraints, performance service-level agreements, and correctness invariants.

**Application.** Physical limits require suitable analysis under explicit corners; performance claims need matched workload measurements with quantified uncertainty. A formal proof can discharge a named correctness invariant under its model and assumptions, while other functional requirements may need simulation, tests, or additional properties. RedHawk-SC can supply power-integrity analysis; a thermal-analysis path must be separately selected and bound before making a thermal claim.

**Outcome.** A requirement remains open if its returned check is unqualified or no check has been assigned to it. For an unqualified return, investigate the qualification gap and repair or rerun the check as needed. Where no check exists, assign a suitable evaluation path. This mapping states what the prospective subsystem would need; it does not report completed Lighthouse verification.
:::

### Matching Each Check to What It Can Actually Observe {#sec-check-fidelity-scoping}

Every tool check in an architecture flow operates within the observational horizon @sec-data-representations-world-models records for its source, and qualification turns that horizon into an explicit boundary on the claim. A syntax linter verifies port lists and grammar without ensuring that logic will synthesize cleanly; a cycle-level simulator measures instruction throughput across modeled queues while remaining blind to physical layout congestion, clock-tree skew, or parasitic wire $RC$ delays.[^fn-rc-delay-c07] Neither a faster proxy upstream nor a clean physical pass downstream widens what a tool can check beyond what its underlying model observes.

[^fn-rc-delay-c07]: **Parasitic RC Delays**: In physical layout, microscopic metal wires have inherent electrical resistance (R) and capacitance (C). Resistance and capacitance set the scale of interconnect delay, while the wire geometry, driver, load, and distributed network determine the path delay. Wire delay can limit timing even when individual logic gates become faster.

Static timing analysis makes that observational boundary concrete. Consider a simplified edge-triggered, single-clock design with a combinational timing graph $G=(V, E)$ in which timing pins are vertices and propagation arcs are edges. The static timing analysis (STA) engine propagates arrival times through this graph under the supplied constraints and corner models. Let $T_{\text{arr, max}}$ measure the worst-case data arrival relative to the launch-clock edge, incorporating maximum clock-to-Q delay, data-path delay, and path-specific on-chip variation derating factors. When positive $t_{\text{skew}}$ means that the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock and $t_{\text{uncertainty}}$ accounts for clock phase jitter and pessimism margins, the setup condition for the latest arrival is:

$$
T_{\text{arr, max}} \le T_{\text{req}} = T_{\text{clk}} - t_{\text{setup}} + t_{\text{skew}} - t_{\text{uncertainty}}
$$

For the hold check, $T_{\text{arr, min}}$ instead denotes the earliest arrival (incorporating minimum clock-to-Q delay, minimum data-path delay, and fast-path on-chip variation derating factors) and must satisfy:

$$
T_{\text{arr, min}} \ge t_{\text{hold}} + t_{\text{skew}} + t_{\text{uncertainty}}
$$

preventing newly launched data from corrupting the captured value during the capture flip-flop's hold interval. In multi-corner multi-mode analysis, setup and hold are usually limited at different corners: setup is typically limited by slow process silicon at reduced supply voltage and hold by fast silicon at elevated voltage, while the limiting temperature depends on the node because temperature inversion at advanced nodes can make low temperature the slow case. A candidate that passes timing under a single nominal corner can therefore fail severely across the full multi-corner envelope. Even across all corners, these inequalities cover only the paths and checks enabled by the model and constraints. A `set_false_path` directive excludes matching paths from the specified timing analysis without establishing that the physical paths meet timing or reporting a meaningful zero slack for them. As in the SDC defect class of @sec-semantic-rtl-defects, an unjustified exception can remove a real violation from the report even while the STA engine follows its inputs without error and the checking setup omits a required obligation.

The same principle applies across the verification stack: what an engine's model contains decides both what its results can support and what they cannot establish on their own (@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What results support under declared conditions** | **What results cannot establish by themselves** |
| - | - | - |
| Syntax and interface | Adherence to schemas, grammatical rules, and port widths. | Functional correctness, performance, power, or physical feasibility. |
| Functional simulation | Execution behavior on explicit software binaries under model semantics. | Timing closure, physical cell layout, thermal stability, and unexecuted paths. |
| Hardware emulation | Long-trace execution behavior at high effective cycle counts. | Final physical timing closure, detailed routing constraints, and power dissipation. |
| Low-power static | UPF power domain intent and structural isolation rules. | Dynamic IR-drop, power-switch settling delays, and active energy consumption. |
| Formal verification | Proofs/counterexamples for explicit properties over bounded/unbounded models. | Objectives outside the property set, or behavior under violated assumptions. |
| Architectural models | Microarchitectural cycle timing for declared workloads (gem5, ChampSim). | Physical layout limits or behaviors outside validated model regions. |
| Physical analysis | Implementation and physical results under specified models: synthesis (Yosys), place-and-route (OpenROAD), physical signoff (geometric design rule checking and layout versus schematic verification via Calibre), STA (Tempus), power integrity (RedHawk-SC), and separately bound thermal analysis. | Missing constraints, functional intent, or unmodeled manufacturing variation. |
| Silicon telemetry | Measured behavior of fabricated parts under test conditions. | Unmeasured workloads, operating lifetimes, or uncharacterized parts. |
: **Checks are decisive only for the properties they observe.** Costlier or downstream tools do not widen property coverage. {#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stronger claims require stronger checks"}
**The principle:** Verification rigor must match the consequences and reversibility of the architectural decision.

**The application:** High-consequence decisions require checks suited to each material claim. Formal proofs, signoff reports, and silicon measurements address different obligations; none substitutes for the others merely because it is more rigorous or costly. Uncalibrated surrogate scores cannot justify such commitments.
:::

In practice, the consequence and reversibility of a decision set the required verification depth (@tbl-feedback-by-consequence). Inner-loop candidate screening tolerates bounded surrogate error because a mistake merely wastes evaluation budget or defers a promising candidate. Revising a shared bus protocol requires checks of the affected behavioral and interface obligations because errors propagate into downstream blocks, and freezing pinouts for tapeout requires full implementation signoff checks because a mistake can force a mask respin and months of delay.

| **Intended use of result** | **Consequence if wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| - | - | - |
| Local candidate screening | Wasted simulation budget or deferred promising candidates. | Candidate identity, matched comparator, and known proxy error bounds. |
| Shared interface revision | Downstream hardware/software work inherits errors. | Regression suites, interface compatibility checks, and explicit assumptions. |
| High-consequence commitment | Mask respin, tapeout failure, and months of schedule delay. | Signoff checks covering all material claims, decision-margin bounds, and independent verifiers. |
: **Feedback plans must follow consequence and reversibility.** Verification rigor matches the cost of error propagation. {#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

Even at signoff, stronger checks reduce specific risks without guaranteeing zero residual risk. Adding more checkers improves confidence only when they contribute independent evidence; if two tools share a flawed assumption, both can miss the same failure.

### Correlated Blind Spots and Diverse Checkers {#sec-correlated-blind-spots}

Running two different tools does not guarantee independent failure behavior, as multiversion-programming research cautions [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. Language-model evaluators can also favor their own generations [@PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference]. For architectural verification, the practical question is which specification assumptions, model simplifications, or learned components the producer and checker share (@fig-independent-checks). Those shared dependencies can leave the same defect unchallenged even when the checks carry different names.

![**A second check provides value only when it challenges an otherwise untested assumption.** Sharing a model or specification between producer and critic produces correlated agreement rather than independent validation (left). A claim-specific check using an orthogonal measurement path mounts a bounded challenge, though unexamined shared assumptions must still be recorded (right) [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion; @PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference].](images/fig-independent-checks){#fig-independent-checks width="80%" fig-alt="Two-column flow diagram contrasting correlated agreement from shared assumptions against a bounded challenge from an orthogonal checking path."}

Whereas @sec-semantic-rtl-defects used mutation testing [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints] to measure whether a single test suite catches deliberately altered programs, applying the same technique across several checkers exposes their joint escapes. When a non-equivalent injected RTL defect escapes both an automated formal assertion suite and a dynamic testbench, the joint escape demonstrates a shared detection gap for that fault. Because both checks may inherit a specification omission or each may miss the fault for a different reason, the verification team must trace the escape through the asserted property, formal assumptions, test stimulus, and checked outputs to decide which check needs revision before rerunning the mutant to confirm that the gap has closed.

Audits of agentic benchmarks point to a related hazard: weak test suites and reward rules that accept empty responses can inflate apparent pass rates [@ZhuEtAl2025AgenticBenchmarks]. In RTL verification, stimulus must exercise the behavior whose correctness is claimed, and the checker must observe its effects. Test vectors that run without exercising internal state transitions (such as testing an arithmetic pipeline with operand streams that never trigger carry generation, overflow saturation, or AXI backpressure valid-ready stalls) create a false impression of high verification pass rates while leaving critical control paths untested.

Hardware security properties expose another shared blind spot. Because Spectre and Meltdown demonstrated leakage through transient execution and microarchitectural side channels that ordinary checks of architectural outputs need not detect [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown], test suites that inspect only architectural outputs can agree while leaving the relevant information-flow property unexamined, for the same reason that inspecting isolated executions cannot establish noninterference (@sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence). When a search loop evaluates an objective based only on throughput or power, performance, and area, it can favor changes to speculation, resource sharing, or hardware mitigations without charging their security cost. Catching those regressions requires checks matched to the threat model, such as a noninterference proof under declared speculative semantics, cache-timing-channel analysis, or a structural check for domain isolation, rather than repeating a functional test that never observes information flow.

## Routing Failures Back to the Layer That Caused Them {#sec-routing-evidence-layers}

Once a check returns a qualified result, that evidence must reach the part of the design process equipped to act on it. A formal counterexample may call for RTL repair or specification revision, once the verification team establishes whether the specification misstates the intended contract or the RTL violates it. Negative timing slack calls for timing diagnosis before choosing a repair, whereas an unresolved empirical delta calls for expanded trace sampling. Because these actions change different objects, collapsing every tool return into a single scalar optimizer score loses the information needed to choose the next step. Similarly, a *distribution shift* changes the workloads, tool versions, or operating conditions that generated the data on which a surrogate or claim was qualified;[^fn-proxy-shift-c07] a known change in those conditions, or deteriorating agreement with new reference measurements, calls for requalifying the affected surrogate rather than continuing to optimize against stale assumptions (@tbl-feedback-destinations).

How much detail a returned signal preserves governs the diagnosis a workflow can make, while the workflow's representation and allowed actions determine which repairs it can attempt. Three classes of returned signal differ in the context they preserve. @tbl-feedback-taxonomy-layers associates each class with the operational layer of @sec-three-operational-layers that most characteristically consumes it; the association is a tendency rather than a rigid boundary, since a Layer 2 flow can also read a signoff report.

1. *Scalar PPA proxies (Layer 2).* Scalar figures of merit compress multidimensional hardware behavior into a single numerical value, such as runtime latency, energy estimates, or composite objective scores ($S = \text{cycles} / \bar{U}$). Such scores can rank candidates for an optimizer, including structural candidates when its search space permits them, but the number alone neither identifies a failing path nor explains why a design improved. Retained diagnostic logs and controlled contrasts supply that context, while checks of omitted objectives remain necessary to catch proxy gaming.
2. *Structured error diagnostics (Layer 1 and Layer 3).* Structured diagnostics include syntax linter trees, AST validation errors, clock-domain crossing violation reports, and formal verification counterexample traces. In Layer 1 workflows, these diagnostics go to a human engineer who absorbs the manual integration tax of debugging and editing the RTL. In a prospective Layer 3 AI-native design system, automated generation and repair components would consume these structured diagnostics directly, using counterexample waveforms to guide AST mutations or abstraction refinement. Published repair loops that operate this way remain point demonstrations, and the end-to-end study examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect does not report how its repairs compare with a matched conventional flow.
3. *Physical signoff traces (Layer 3).* Authoritative physical signoff tools (static timing analysis, dynamic IR-drop analysis, design rule checking, and layout-versus-schematic verification) produce multidimensional traces detailing launch-to-capture path delays, cell-level slew rates, spatial metal-layer current densities, and geometric layout coordinates. Within the bounds of their models, corners, and constraints, these physical traces provide pre-silicon evidence that could guide diagnosis across the causal repair hierarchy in a Layer 3 system. Choosing whether to apply a localized physical ECO, insert pipeline registers, or restructure a subsystem still requires verifying that the proposed repair fixes the violation without breaking other requirements.

| **Operational layer** | **Primary feedback class** | **Verification and evaluation oracles** | **Degrees of freedom ($\Theta$)** | **Feedback routing destination** | **Characteristic failure mode** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Layer 1: point assistance** | Structured error diagnostics and compiler logs | Syntax linters, unit testbenches, and manual code review | Local artifact or task within human-directed workflow | Human engineer absorbing integration tax | Self-verification paradox and unexercised corner cases |
| **Layer 2: container-bound optimization** | Scalar PPA proxies and surrogate metrics | Cycle simulators (gem5, SCALE-Sim) and learned PPA estimators | Parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$ inside immutable template | Numerical optimizer (Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning (RL)) | Proxy gaming, Goodhart's law, and Whac-a-Mole regressions |
| **Layer 3: AI-native design system** | Physical signoff traces, with structured diagnostics such as formal counterexamples | Authoritative signoff tools (Tempus, RedHawk-SC, Calibre, JasperGold) | Joint hardware-software structure across layers (prospective) | Causal repair hierarchy and topological refactoring engines | Exponential verification timeouts and solver state-space explosion |
: **Each operational layer characteristically consumes a different class of feedback.** The returned signal supplies diagnostic context, while the representation and allowed actions determine which repairs a workflow can attempt; the Layer 3 row describes what an AI-native design system would need to consume, not an established workflow. {#tbl-feedback-taxonomy-layers tbl-colwidths="[14,20,20,18,14,14]"}

[^fn-proxy-shift-c07]: **Proxy Gaps and Shift**: In ML terminology, covariate shift changes the input distribution while preserving the conditional distribution of the target given the inputs. A change in that conditional relationship is a different shift. Which description fits a workload or process change depends on the model's inputs and prediction target; the node name alone does not decide it.

| **Qualified or verified status** | **Implicated architectural object** | **Eligible next technical action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy outside support** | Method choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or halt proxy use. Do not treat unsupported proxy outputs as training labels. |
| **Missing constraint** | Study formulation or representation | Record rationale and add missing constraint to representation. |
| **Resolved outcome, open mechanism** | Study formulation | Preserve result and add a distinguishing contrast before attributing the outcome to a mechanism. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan | Use further investigation allowed by the declared plan, or define a new comparison with its own budget and stopping rule. |
| **Difference below decision margin** | Study findings | Retain result without forcing architectural or model updates. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Design requirements and responsible owner | Record waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, and reopening trigger. |
: **Established status determines next technical actions.** Execution failures route to environment repairs; qualified results direct changes to the representation, study, or retained findings. {#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

When checkers disagree, the conflict needs diagnosis before it drives a design change. If a formal run reports Proved while simulation shows a miscompare, the verification team must determine whether the formal proof actually covers the failing behavior under the simulation's inputs and assumptions. Similarly, if two proxies rank a pair of candidates in opposite orders without either ranking identifying the cause, the team must examine each proxy's scope, reference agreement, and uncertainty using @tbl-proxy-diagnostics. Until the discrepancy is explained, both returns and their qualified limits stay on the record, the disputed behavior or ranking is withheld from training labels, and only independently qualified reference measurements remain usable within their established scope.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Drive actions only from qualified results"}
**The principle:** Raw simulation logs and unparsed tool reports must never directly trigger design modifications or dataset updates.

**The application:** Only qualified statuses justify repairs, revisions, no-change decisions, or technical stops. A declared method's own update rule, such as a Bayesian optimizer's posterior update on an admitted measurement, is a qualified use; a surrogate score or an unparsed log entering the same update is not.
:::

Even when a qualified check confirms a real violation, the appropriate action is sometimes a bounded waiver rather than an immediate redesign. Siemens Calibre Auto-Waivers provides a concrete example of retaining and applying geometric design-rule waivers across layout iterations [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. In the discipline proposed here, each accepted exception records its technical rationale, the affected rule and design scope (including spatial coordinates or identifying geometry where relevant), any compensating controls, the responsible owner, and the reopening trigger. A waiver documents a bounded exception; it does not turn the underlying violation into an unconditional pass.

## Updating Search Models and Constraints After Each Run {#sec-propagating-feedback-optimizer}

Routing qualified evidence determines what to retain about the design, but the same evidence can also change how the search proposes its next candidate. Those two uses of feedback must remain distinct: a verified timing failure belongs permanently in the study's findings, while the optimizer may also use it to update a surrogate or steer toward another design. Allowing unverified returns, transient execution errors, or biased candidate distributions into the optimizer state can mislead subsequent proposals [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden; @Settles2009ActiveLearning].

Managing optimizer updates starts with separating adaptation within a declared method from replacing that method. Updating a Bayesian optimizer's posterior after a qualified measurement is part of its normal operation and does not require a separate model-promotion study after every observation, provided the update rule, admitted measurements, and resulting state remain inspectable. Changing the surrogate family, generator prompt, or search policy alters the method being evaluated and requires a separate comparison before the revised version guides further work.

One practical way to manage method replacements is to stage proposed versions in a separate, versioned candidate-model store apart from the active search (@tbl-retention-vs-quarantine). Each staged version retains its training data, settings, and intended use so that a head-to-head comparison against the active version can test whether the change improves the relevant outcome: prediction error and screening decisions for a surrogate, or candidate quality and total evaluation cost for a generator or policy. Because a version that fails to improve on the declared criterion simply remains inactive, this store provides a clean testbed for method changes rather than a hurdle for routine within-run updates.

| **Dimension** | **Retained design findings** | **Search state and proposed method changes** |
| - | - | - |
| **Storage** | Existing experiment records, verification reports, and decision history. | Versioned search state; a separate registry for proposed replacement models or policies where useful. |
| **Contents** | Passed, failed, and inconclusive checks with their scope, assumptions, and candidate identities. | Surrogate weights, generator prompts, search trajectories, and the measurements admitted to each update. |
| **Integrity and qualification** | Version identities preserve traceability; technical checks establish what the findings support. | Declared update rules govern within-run adaptation; comparisons assess proposed method replacements. |
| **Reopening trigger** | Changed process corner, tool behavior, or ISA assumptions; license availability separately affects whether a rerun can execute. | Changed input conditions, or drift in residuals or empirical interval coverage measured against reference results. |
: **Design findings and search updates have different jobs.** Retained evidence records what was checked, while versioned search state makes the use of that feedback inspectable. A proposed method change still needs evaluation suited to its intended use. {#tbl-retention-vs-quarantine tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Neither a separate registry nor an integrity hash establishes technical validity on its own. An unsupported surrogate score cannot become a verified training label merely because it was stored in a registry, and a timing waiver still needs a technical rationale and an authorized scope because its file hash only identifies the artifact. Even when evaluation cases are kept out of training, repeatedly testing proposed models against the same holdout can leak information through the promotion decisions themselves. The study must therefore limit that adaptive reuse, refresh the confirmation cases, or use an inference procedure designed for reuse rather than assuming a static holdout remains independent indefinitely [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

Changes in workloads, tool versions, or PVT corners can invalidate the qualification on which dependent architectural claims rest [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. Conformal prediction makes the need for fresh reference measurements particularly clear: its standard interval guarantee assumes exchangeability of the calibration examples and the candidate being predicted, meaning that permuting them does not change their joint distribution.[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07] Moving to a new workload regime can violate that assumption, whether it induces covariate shift that preserves the conditional target distribution given the inputs or alters that conditional relationship outright. Adaptive selection breaks exchangeability in a second way, because choosing candidates for extreme predicted performance systematically favors optimistic prediction errors. In either case, losing the theoretical marginal guarantee does not automatically mean actual coverage has collapsed, just as @sec-support-limits noted that split-conformal intervals do not automatically extend to an adaptively selected finalist, but checking how the intervals behave requires new reference measurements under the shifted conditions.

Although rolling empirical coverage measured against reference runs can reveal deteriorating coverage, that monitor observes only the candidates routed to reference tools. A known change in operating conditions is therefore reason enough to revisit qualification immediately rather than wait for a coverage alarm. Once the surrogate goes back through the proxy diagnostics of @tbl-proxy-diagnostics and matched reference measurements are taken at the new stratum, its scores earn trust again only within the region those measurements cover. Widening a reported interval by hand does not restore its coverage guarantee, whereas tracing claims to exact execution bindings limits the rerun work to the checks actually affected by the shift.

[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07]: **Conformal prediction prerequisites**: The standard finite-sample marginal guarantee assumes exchangeability of calibration and test examples. Weighted conformal prediction can address covariate shift under its own assumptions, including the unchanged conditional target distribution and suitable knowledge of the covariate likelihood ratio [@TibshiraniEtAl2019CovariateShift]. It is not a general remedy for arbitrary adaptive selection or conditional shift. Fresh calibration under a suitable sampling design or a method justified for the particular selection process may be needed; widening intervals without such an argument does not restore the guarantee.

How a workflow updates its search state during a run depends on its design representation and allowed actions (@tbl-feedback-taxonomy-layers). In a Layer 2 search over a fixed parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$, admitted measurements update a surrogate's Gaussian-process posterior or a reinforcement-learning policy. A prospective Layer 3 AI-native design system would also need to represent and check changes to structure and interfaces. While one proposed approach turns recurring formal counterexamples into candidate invariants or architectural constraints, and a failing trace can also guide a generator directly, repairing that single trace does not prove that structurally similar violations have been prevented; the revised design still must be checked against the intended contract. Similarly, although a routing-congestion report can motivate a floorplan constraint or topology change that then undergoes fresh physical checks, the studies examined here do not show that automated cross-layer repair outperforms a matched conventional process.

What a qualified result should change depends on how far ahead it reaches across three time horizons. Within a single run, it guides the next candidate proposal or check. Across an ongoing project, it updates the design record when a Proved status discharges a scoped requirement, a waiver enters with its reopening trigger, or a difference inside the decision margin is retained without forcing a change. Across future projects, the reusable assets extend well beyond surrogate weights or a winning parameter configuration: the check that caught a subtle defect, the mutant set that exposed a vacuous testbench, and the conditions under which a proxy was calibrated can all guide a new study, provided each is requalified in that setting.

## Open Questions {#sec-feedback-open-questions}

Turning raw tool outputs into trusted architectural evidence exposes five open research problems as automated search alters the candidates, interfaces, and failure modes under test:

- **When an optimizer pushes designs right up to the clock-timing limit, how do we keep a fast timing model from letting failing paths slip through?** Standard regression losses and split-conformal intervals treat 50\ ps of optimism and 50\ ps of pessimism as equally bad, yet in hardware screening an optimistic error lets a setup violation pass while a pessimistic error merely rejects a borderline candidate or triggers an extra static-timing run. Because an optimizer actively hunts for candidates pressed against the zero-slack boundary, it systematically picks designs where the predictor was overly optimistic, breaking the exchangeability assumption behind standard coverage guarantees. We still lack practical ways to build one-sided calibration bounds and targeted reference-sampling rules that limit false passes along an active search frontier, keeping pre-signoff screening reliable without mistaking a calibrated surrogate for a signoff static timing analyzer.

- **When a model helps write both the hardware and the testbench, how do we catch the blind spots they share?** Joint mutation testing can expose bugs that slip past both a dynamic simulation testbench and a formal assertion suite, but small syntax mutants injected into an existing abstract syntax tree still share any specification omission inherited by both the RTL and its checkers, much as independent teams in multiversion avionics software repeatedly coded the same boundary bugs when working from a shared ambiguous specification. That correlated failure risk sharpens when a language model drafts an RTL module alongside its testbench or SystemVerilog assertions, or when a structural search introduces an interface protocol that the original verification plan never anticipated. We still need specification-level fault models and independent contract-synthesis methods that test shared assumptions directly and place statistical bounds on the bugs that remain beyond a finite set of injected mutants.

- **How can we catch dangerous power-up current spikes at the RTL or floorplan stage, before a full physical layout exists?** Static Unified Power Format (UPF) checks and low-power RTL simulations quickly verify isolation clamping and power-state tables, but they cannot see the inrush currents, ground bounce, and dynamic voltage droop that occur when multiple power domains wake up simultaneously. Because a structural search cannot afford full-chip place-and-route and dynamic IR-drop simulation on every proposed power-domain partition, it needs a fast way to rule out electrically unsafe wakeup schedules early. We do not yet have conservative pre-layout current-envelope models that can flag hazardous domain-transition sequences at RTL or floorplan time while clearly marking the switching regimes where the early bound is inconclusive and full physical signoff must run.

- **When a check fails at the boundary between two hardware blocks, how can an automated repair loop tell whether the bug lies inside one block or in the interface contract between them?** In compositional assume-guarantee verification, a counterexample trace at a module boundary can stem from an internal state-machine bug, an upstream driver violating its assumed traffic envelope, or an interface contract that is too weak to prevent deadlock under realistic backpressure. Patching a block's local RTL when the contract itself is flawed wastes synthesis cycles and risks breaking neighboring blocks, whereas escalating every assertion failure to a full interface redesign destroys modularity. We still lack diagnostic synthesis and counterfactual trace-slicing methods that can tell when a violation can be fixed strictly inside a block's existing contract and when the system must instead renegotiate the assume-guarantee boundary across adjacent subsystems.

- **When several verification tools overlap in what they test, how do we decide whether running one more checker is worth the compute and license cost?** Adding a formal property engine, a mutation-testing pass, or an extra timing corner can catch defects that earlier stages missed, but each added check consumes compute servers and commercial license seats while partially duplicating existing coverage and introducing its own false rejections. Because checkers often share specification assumptions, simple majority voting among evaluators can reinforce a shared blind spot rather than reduce risk, and historical fault-kill ratios measured on baseline designs often break down once a generator shifts the candidate distribution. We still lack practical verification scheduling rules that estimate how much new evidence an extra check will provide on the current candidate, allocating tool budgets to balance missed-defect risk against false-rejection cost.

## Summary {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

A tool return becomes usable architectural evidence when its candidate identity, operating conditions, execution status, and observational scope support the claim being made. For a formal result, qualification binds the property to its model, assumptions, and proof status; for a comparative measurement, it also requires a matched comparator, quantified uncertainty, and a declared decision margin. Keeping those requirements distinct lets an architect preserve a valid proof even when a performance comparison remains unresolved, or retain a measured latency gain without claiming unbounded correctness.

Once a return is qualified, its status determines the eligible next action. A formal counterexample can justify an RTL repair or a revised architectural proposal, an unresolved comparison can justify collecting more measurements under the declared plan, and a discrepancy between checkers calls for diagnosis before either result changes the design. Learning then operates across three horizons: guiding the next proposal or check within the active run, updating the findings retained across the project, and carrying proven checks or calibration limits forward to later studies. Within a run, routine updates follow the declared method, whereas proposed replacement models or policies require evaluation before adoption, and unsupported surrogate scores are never treated as verified training labels because each retained finding carries the conditions under which it can be reused.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Repair needs both an available action and evidence to assess it.** The represented search space determines which changes a loop can propose. Scalar scores can rank those proposals, while structured diagnostics add context for diagnosis. A proposed structural repair still needs checks of its intended effect and the requirements it may invalidate.
- **A passing suite shows only that it caught the faults tested.** Use claim-specific verification paths and seeded faults to test whether agreement reflects genuine fault detection. A passing mutant suite qualifies detection of the tested faults; shared omissions can remain.
- **Only qualified returns should drive the next action.** Admit measurements under the criteria of @tbl-measurement-record and formal returns under their property, model, assumptions, and status, and route each according to the scoped claim it supports. License preemption, cluster timeouts, and environment crashes route to environment repair rather than becoming false design failures.
- **Proof and measurement answer different questions.** A completed unbounded proof establishes that an invariant holds across all reachable states within its declared assumptions. A comparative trade-off needs matched conditions, qualified workload and model scope, and a decision margin declared before measurement. Sampling or run variation also requires appropriate uncertainty characterization, such as a confidence interval; an exact deterministic score does not require a sampling interval.
- **Updating the search is a different job from retaining evidence.** Preserve checked findings with their conditions, and record how they update the search. Separate ordinary adaptation under the declared method from proposed model or policy replacements, whose benefit still needs evaluation.
:::

Which of those findings, checks, and surrogates remain valid when the workload, toolchain, or process node changes is a question of transfer across problems rather than adaptation within a single run, and @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack takes up that challenge next.
